segments.narration: Hundreds of thousands of shooting stars turned the night sky into fire. On November 13, 1833, North America witnessed a massive and intense meteor storm.
For hours, up to one hundred thousand blazing streaks fell every single hour. Campfires paled against the sudden illumination, and sleeping travelers bolted upright in sheer terror.
Was the solar system collapsing right before their eyes?
Yale astronomer Denison Olmsted tracked the paths of the falling light. He proved the meteors didn't fall at random, but all radiated outward from a single point in the constellation Leo.
Earth had simply plunged through a dense trail of dust left behind by past passages of the Tempel-Tuttle comet. The apocalypse was just an ancient trail of space debris.

accuracy_flags.claim: Trillions of shooting stars lit up the night sky across North America in November 1833.
accuracy_flags.note: The article states peak rates were over one hundred thousand meteors an hour (or estimated in excess of 240,000 during nine hours), not 'trillions'.

accuracy_flags.claim: The incredible light show was caused by Earth passing through the debris trail of Comet Tempel-Tuttle.
accuracy_flags.note: The reference article explicitly states that the 1833 storm was from a direct impact with the previous 1800 dust trail, not a direct passage of the comet itself.
